The first difference, in the decision boundaries, is the 530 larger one, and is not an effect of the illusions. In the 531 model, it is a matter of caution: users required more ev-532 idence before responding, so they responded later and 533 erred less. Age is an obvious candidate explanation. Both an illusion. None of the other differences was explained by age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the reported intensity of the last experience.

The second difference is the one that bears on the predictive-processing account, with three indices used to describe it (Table 3). The first is the illusion's effect on discriminability, which measures how much the illusory context reduces the drift of the evidence towards the correct response. This effect did not differ between the groups: the illusion cost users as much discriminability as naïve participants. Users' discriminability, however, changed more with the real difference between the targets, so that the same illusory effect weighed less against it. The attitudes and well-being have been documented long after one or a few doses (Aday et al., 2020; Knudsen, 2023), and long-term ayahuasca users differed from matched controls in the thickness of the posterior cingulate cortex, to a degree that followed the intensity and duration of their use (Bouso et al., 2015). A lasting change in perception would be of the same kind. It would, however, be expected to grow with use, and we found no relation between the illusion magnitude and the lifetime number of uses. A second interpretation is that of a difference that was there before, in the people who choose to use psychedelics: in perceptual style, in familiarity with altered perception, or in how they approach a visual task. A third is that of some other difference between the two populations. Our 612 cross-sectional design cannot tell them apart.

613

These results also differ from those of the acute studies.

Geo-624 metrical illusions have also been related to earlier stages of 625 visual processing (Morgan et al., 1990; Schwarzkopf et al., 626 2011), although the relation with the surface area of the 627 primary visual cortex was not replicated (Jastrzębowska 628 et al., 2026). Nor do they behave as one phenomenon. 629 Susceptibility is typically only weakly correlated between 630 illusions (Cretenoud et al., 2019; Jastrzębowska et al., 631 2026), even if some similarity between geometrical il-632 lusions has been reported (Axelrod et al., 2017), and 633 susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion, but not to the 634 Ebbinghaus illusion, varies with autistic traits (Chouinard 635 et al., 2013) and with age during development (Navarrete 636 et al., 2025). Our data agree. The illusion magnitude was 637 only moderately correlated across the three illusions, and 638 its reduction in users ranged from 15% on the Müller-Lyer 639 illusion to 34% on the Ebbinghaus illusion. A difference 640 between users and non-users may therefore not have the 641 same origin for each illusion. 642 The study has several limitations. The design is cross-643 sectional, and the groups were recruited through different 644 routes. Every difference between users and naïve partic-645 ipants is therefore confounded with age, education, lan-646 guage and whatever else draws a person to a psychedelic 647 society. The groups overlap in age in only a few partici-648 pants, so we did not adjust the model for age. Instead, we 649 reported what age and the other covariates account for, 650 and relied on the comparison of recent with past users, 651 which holds them constant.

The sample is modest and its 652 size was not planned for a given power. Psychedelic use 653 was self-reported and not verified, and the 30-day window 654 groups together experiences with different substances, 655 doses and settings. Testing was online, on displays that we 656 did not control. The model reproduces the error rates and 657 the median response times closely, but predicts a longer 658 tail of slow errors than observed. Its boundary separation 659 and start point were allowed to vary with illusion strength 660 and task difficulty, like its other parameters, although the 661 trials were mixed within blocks, so that participants could 662 not set them for the coming trial. These terms may there-663 fore absorb effects of the stimulus that the drift rate alone 664 does not capture.

665

In sum, people who use classic psychedelics did this 666 task more cautiously and more accurately than younger, 667 psychedelic-naïve adults, and were somewhat less sensitive 668 to the illusions, adjusting for perceptual performance. This second finding is in the direction that relaxed priors would predict, but it characterises the population of users and not the recent dose. Whether a dose produces it, and for how long, is a question for future within-subject designs that measure the illusion magnitude before and after.

Second, 69 each stimulus is generated from two parameters that vary 70 independently and continuously. The task difficulty is the 71 real (objective) difference between the two targets: the 72 smaller the difference, the harder the trial. The illusion 73 strength is the magnitude of the context that biases how 74 the targets look, and this context can work in favour of 75 the real difference, which makes the task easier, or against 76 it, which makes it harder. The effect of the illusion can 77 therefore be separated from the ability to tell the targets 78 apart. Third, choices and response times can be modelled 79 together with an evidence accumulation model (Ratcliff 80 & McKoon, 2008), which describes performance by a 81 few parameters and estimates how each of them changes 82 with the illusion separately from its level without one. In 83 addition to these parameters, we computed an index to fa-84 cilitate comparisons between groups that differ in average 85 performance. Because the real difference varies as well, 86the effect of the illusion can be expressed relative to that 87 of the real difference, that is, as the real difference that the 88 illusion is equivalent to. 162 the Ebbinghaus illusion, two red circles are 170 shown side by side, each surrounded by black circles, 171 and the participant says which red circle is bigger.

A 172 circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller, so the 173 illusion strength is the relative size of the surrounding 174 circles. In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two horizontal red 175 lines are shown one above the other, with black fins at their 176 ends, and the participant says which line is longer. The 177 illusion strength is the angle of the fins: the more they are 178 tilted, the stronger the illusion. In the vertical-horizontal 179 illusion, two red lines are shown side by side, one of 180 them rotated towards the vertical, and the participant says 181 which is longer. Lines closer to the vertical look longer, 182 so the illusion strength is the angle of rotation: the larger 183 the rotation, the stronger the illusion. 193

Each illusion had a practice block of 8 trials and two test blocks of 80 trials, which gives 480 test trials in all. Trials were in random order within a block. The order of the illusions (Müller-Lyer, Ebbinghaus, 199 vertical-horizontal) was the same in both series of test blocks and for every participant, so that it cannot differ between the groups. After each test block, participants were shown a score combining their speed and accuracy (derived from their mean correct response time divided by their proportion of correct responses). The Illusion Game followed the self-association task, and the AAQ-II and DASS-21 (see Questionnaires) were completed between its first and second series of test blocks.

208

Each illusion used 20 illusion strengths (10 facilitating and 10 conflicting) and 8 real differences, split between its two blocks. The real difference is relative: the larger target exceeded the smaller one by 5 to 50% in the Ebbinghaus illusion, by 4.5 to 45% in the Müller-Lyer illusion and by 3 to 30% in the vertical-horizontal illusion. At the strongest illusions, the surrounding circles were 150% larger than the circle they surrounded, the fins were tilted by 30 degrees and the line was rotated by 45 degrees. The stimuli were images of 800 by 800 pixels, shown at that size in full-screen mode. Their physical size therefore depended on the display, but the real differences, being relative, did not. Both predictors were normalized: Illusion strength runs from -1 (the strongest facilitating illusion) through 0 (no 223 illusion) to +1 (the strongest conflicting illusion). Task difficulty runs from -1 (the largest difference shown, the easiest trials) to +1 (the smallest, the hardest trials), so that the whole range of difficulty spans 2 units. Questionnaires Psychological flexibility was measured with the seven-229 item Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II [AAQ-230 II; Bond et al. (2011); French version by Monestès et al. (2009)]. Its score is the sum of the items, each rated from 1 to 7, and a higher score means less flexibility (Cronbach's α in this sample = 0.91, as for the values that follow). Distress was measured with the 21-item 235 Depression Anxiety Stress Scales [DASS-21; Lovibond and Lovibond (1995)]. Each subscale score is the mean of its seven items, rated from 0 to 3, and the total is the mean of the three subscales (α = 0.93 for the total, 0.88, 239 0.80 and 0.87 for Depression, Anxiety and Stress). Figure 2 A illustrates. After a non-decision time 𝜏 , which covers encoding the stimulus and executing the response, evidence accumulates noisily between two boundaries, one for the correct response and one for the error, until it reaches one of them, which determines the decision. The model has five parameters. The drift rate 𝑣 is the average rate at which the evidence moves towards the correct response; it is negative when the evidence favours the error. The boundary separation 𝑎 is the amount of evidence gathered before responding: wider boundaries make responses slower and errors rarer, so it measures caution. The start point 𝑤 is where the accumulation begins, as a share of 𝑎 from the correct boundary (0.5 is unbiased). The non-decision time 𝜏 is the time outside the decision, and the drift variability 𝑠 𝑣 is the standard ,200 participants per illusion.

The effect of the illusion 350 is the change in a quantity from no illusion (strength 0) 351 to the strongest conflicting illusion (strength 1), at mid 352 difficulty. For the parameters, this is their slope on illusion 353 strength, computed with estimate_slopes(). The third 6 MAKOWSKI ET AL. contrast is the illusion magnitude, defined as the effect of illusion strength on discriminability relative to the effect of task difficulty. It is computed from two slopes of discriminability, both taken at no illusion and mid difficulty, where 𝑣(𝑠, 𝑑) is the drift rate at strength 𝑠 and difficulty 𝑑. The first is the slope on illusion strength, 𝑏 𝑠 = 𝑣(1, 0) -𝑣(0, 0): how much discriminability the strongest conflicting illusion removes. The second is the slope on task difficulty, 𝑏 𝑑 = 𝑣(0, 1) -𝑣(0, 0): how much discriminability is lost per unit of difficulty. Both slopes are negative. Their ratio, 𝑏 𝑠 /𝑏 𝑑 , is the number of units of task difficulty that one unit of illusion strength is worth. It corresponds to the shift of the point of subjective equality, expressed in the units of the task. This ratio is independent from overall task performance. user groups were about twelve years older than the naïve 535 group, and older adults have been reported to set wider 536 boundaries and to have longer non-decision times (Ratcliff 10 MAKOWSKI ET AL.

second is the illusion's effect on errors, which measures how often the illusion turns a correct judgement into an error. This effect was smaller in users on the Ebbinghaus illusion, less clearly so on the vertical-horizontal illusion, and similar on the Müller-Lyer illusion. Only the Ebbinghaus illusion, then, reliably led users to the wrong answer less often. The third is the illusion magnitude, which expresses the illusion's effect as the real difference between the targets that it is equivalent to, like the shift of the point of subjective equality in psychophysics. It was smaller in both user groups, on every illusion, which suggests that users' perception of the targets was less biased by the illusion. The three indices thus answer different questions. The first two describe what the illusion does to the evidence and to the response, whereas the illusion magnitude describes the size of the perceptual bias, which is what REBUS makes predictions about. By this index, users were less sensitive to the illusions, and none of the covariates that we measured changed it. Although this is the direction that REBUS predicts, the pattern across the groups was not what we expected. Recent users did not differ from past users in their sensitivity to the illusions, and the illusion magnitude was unrelated to the intensity of the last experience, to the time since it and to the lifetime number of uses. If priors relaxed for days after a dose and then recovered, the illusions would be smaller in recent users and not in past users. What we observe instead is a difference between a population of psychedelic users and a population of young controls, most of them students, whether the last use was weeks or years ago. One interpretation is that of a lasting change after psychedelic use. Enduring changes in personality, not differ from controls on a bodily illusion (Harduf et al., 617 2023).

616

Our users were tested days to years after their last 618 dose, and a different measure was used in each of these 619 studies, so the results do not contradict one another. But to-620 gether they give little support to a single account in which 621 psychedelics weaken illusions by relaxing priors. Such an 622
